title: The months have themes
hook: January the Holy Name, March Joseph, May Mary, June the Sacred Heart, October the rosary, November the dead

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christ the King, crowned with thorns. Your line was king on a cross. Who rules your time, when you looked honestly? Day six hundred eighty-nine.

We've walked the whole Catholic year now, feast by feast: Advent to Christmas, Lent to Easter, Pentecost, the summer saints, all the way to Christ the King. But underneath the feasts, there's a second, quieter calendar that a lot of Catholic grandmothers know by heart. Not days. Months. Ask one what May is for and she won't hesitate. Ask about June, or November. Each month has its own devotion, and for many families it shapes what's on the shelf, what's prayed at night, and what the children bring to school.
screen: `THE WHOLE YEAR, FEAST BY FEAST.` → `A SECOND, QUIETER CALENDAR.` → `MONTHS, NOT DAYS.`

segments.voice: First, what this isn't. The month themes aren't part of the official liturgical calendar. No rule requires them; the Mass doesn't change because it's May. They're popular devotions, grown up over the last few centuries and encouraged by popes, and customs vary from country to country. With that said, here's the common pattern. January, the Holy Name of Jesus, the name given at his circumcision on the eighth day after Christmas. March, Saint Joseph, whose feast falls on the nineteenth. May, Mary. May devotions spread from Italy in the 1700s: flowers before her statue, a May crowning where a child sets a wreath on Mary's head. June, the Sacred Heart, since its feast usually falls then. July, often the Precious Blood. October, the rosary, after the Lepanto feast on the seventh and Leo XIII's letters. November, the holy souls, the dead, opening with All Saints and All Souls. You can feel what the months are doing. They follow the feasts, and stretch a single day into a season of attention. And they map onto ordinary life: Mary in spring flowers, the dead as the leaves come down in the north. A line from Ecclesiastes, in the Douay-Rheims, fits the whole idea: "All things have their season, and in their times all things pass under heaven." A month is long enough to form a habit. That's the point. The feast is the door; the month is the room behind it.
screen: `NOT OFFICIAL; POPULAR DEVOTION.` · `JANUARY TO MARCH: NAME, JOSEPH.` · `MAY, JUNE: MARY, THE HEART.` · `OCTOBER, NOVEMBER: BEADS, THE DEAD.` · then, large: `ALL THINGS HAVE THEIR SEASON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name this month's devotion. Think: what month is it right now? Which of today's themes belongs to it, or the nearest one if it isn't on the list? Then choose one small sign of it for the rest of the month: a flower for May, a picture for June, beads by the bed for October, a list of names for November. If you pray, you can offer the month. If you don't, simply notice the season you're in. The bell holds the time.
The months have themes. A popular Catholic custom, not a rule, giving each month a devotion: the Holy Name, Joseph, Mary, the Sacred Heart, the rosary, the dead. Today's word.
Your line: every month a door. Today, put this month's small sign somewhere you'll pass it every day. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Catholics follow traditional monthly devotions, such as May for Mary with May crownings, June for the Sacred Heart, October for the rosary and November for the dead; these are popular customs, not part of the official liturgical calendar.

fork.setup: it's May, and a parish child asks if the Mass will be different because it's Mary's month. what's the honest answer?
options: yes, every Mass in May is a Mary Mass.
no; the month themes are devotions, not liturgical rules.
fork.reveal: the Mass follows the liturgical calendar. the month's theme lives in devotions: flowers, May crownings, prayers at home.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Church assigns every month an official theme.
what it means: a popular custom that stretches each feast into a month of attention.
what a scholar hears: devotions that grew mostly from the 1700s and 1800s, encouraged by popes, varying by country, outside the liturgical books.

sources.quoted: All things have their season, and in their times all things pass under heaven.

sources.ref: Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy (2001), nos. 190–191 (May), 166–173 (Sacred Heart)

notes: Month devotions vary by source and country; the list follows the outline plus July (Precious Blood). Some lists give February to the Holy Family, April to the Holy Spirit or Eucharist, August to the Immaculate Heart, September to Our Lady of Sorrows, December to the Immaculate Conception.
May devotion origins: commonly traced to 18th-century Italy (Jesuit Annibale Dionisi, 1726; Alfonso Muzzarelli, 1785); confirm.
Directory on Popular Piety paragraph numbers to confirm.
